2025-07-26 09:08:52,576 [INFO] Field changed at answer: '<p>The best solutions to enhance both the <strong>performance</strong> and <strong>resilience</strong> of the website involve making the storage and compute layers more scalable and reliable.</p><ul><li><strong>Copy the website images to an Amazon EFS file system and mount EFS to all relevant EC2 instances.</strong> EFS provides a shared, scalable file system that multiple EC2 instances can mount concurrently, overcoming single-node bottlenecks and failures. It ensures images are not stored on a single instance’s EBS volume, allowing for improved availability and seamless scaling across instances.</li><li><strong>Launch new EC2 instances using an AMI created from the current instance, place them behind an Application Load Balancer within an Auto Scaling group (minimum two instances), and set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the website.</strong> This combination introduces high availability by removing the single EC2 instance failure point, allows for easy scaling based on demand, and leverages CloudFront’s caching to enhance performance and decrease load times for global users.</li></ul><p>Here’s why the other choices are not ideal:</p><ul><li><i>Use an NFS share provided by the main EC2 instance…</i> keeps the architecture dependent on a single EC2 instance for image storage, introducing a potential single point of failure and limiting scalability.</li><li><i>Migrate the website images into an S3 bucket and mount this bucket on each EC2 instance.</i> While S3 is excellent for storing static assets, 'mounting' S3 buckets on EC2 is not natively supported for direct file system operations; using EFS is the preferred shared file system for this use case.</li><li><i>Provision new EC2 instances from an AMI… and configure AWS Global Accelerator…</i> While Global Accelerator improves global edge routing and availability, it does not address the need for a scalable, concurrent solution for shared image storage between EC2 instances, nor offer the caching benefits of CloudFront.</li></ul><p><strong>Tip:</strong> Use Amazon EFS for file sharing across EC2 instances, and always consider CloudFront for accelerating content delivery and reducing origin load. Always tailor permissions tightly to needed actions and the required resource scope.<br><br><b>Tip:</b> Always specify permissions at the most granular level necessary to follow the principle of least privilege, especially in environments with tight security mandates.</p>'

Each shard in Kinesis Data Streams provides fixed write and read capacity limits (1 MB/sec and 1,000 records/sec for writes, and 2 MB/sec for reads). By estimating the peak rate at which records are written to (incoming) and read from (outgoing) your stream, you can select enough shards to meet those needs.</p><p>The incorrect options, <i>"Outgoing write bandwidth"</i> and <i>"Incoming read bandwidth"</i>, are misleading because Kinesis does not support 'writes' on the outgoing side—data is only read out, not written. Always account for both how much data you'll put into the stream (write) and how much you'll need to read out by consumers (read) when estimating your shard count.</p><p><b>Tip:</b> Consider future growth and possible traffic spikes by slightly over-provisioning shards, and monitor metrics post-deployment to make scaling adjustments as needed.</p>' \u2192 '<p>The appropriate metrics for determining the initial shard count in an AWS Kinesis stream are <b>&quot;Incoming write bandwidth&quot;</b> and <b>&quot;Outgoing read bandwidth&quot;</b>. This means not all instances are new during deployment. Some get updated in-place or replaced incrementally.<br> - <em>All at once deployment</em> quickly updates every instance in your environment—often using the <em>same existing</em> EC2 instances—thereby risking downtime and not guaranteeing fresh new instances.<br> - <em>Linear deployment</em> is similar to rolling deployment, just with a consistently-sized batch each time. By doing this, each segment is handled independently and can utilize separate read throughput, significantly reducing the risk of throttling. Splitting scans in parallel is the DynamoDB-recommended best practice for large datasets.</p><p><b>Tip:</b> Consider using Query operations alongside parallel scans when possible, as Queries are more efficient. <ul>

  <li><i>"Messages sent to the topic are distributed across all subscribed queues in a load-balanced manner."</i> is incorrect because SNS does not load-balance messages among subscribed SQS queues—it duplicates messages so every queue gets every published message.</li>
  <li><i>"Subscriptions deliver messages to each SQS queue but with an intentional delay between deliveries."</i> is wrong because SNS attempts near-immediate (asynchronous) delivery to each subscribed SQS queue without a required delay between them.</li>

While <i>Precision</i> measures how many predicted positives are actually positive, and <i>Recall</i> measures how many actual positives are correctly identified, the <b>PR Curve</b> provides a full picture by showing the trade-off between Precision and Recall across various thresholds. This is especially important in imbalanced datasets like yours, where maximizing true positive identification is critical. </p><p><i>ROC Curve</i> is less useful here as it can overestimate performance in datasets dominated by negatives. <i>Recall</i> alone doesn't show how precise those positive predictions are, while <i>Precision</i> alone doesn't account for all true positives that the model can find. It's particularly useful for imbalanced datasets, which is common in seismic event classification tasks.</p><p><i>'Recall rate'</i> only measures the proportion of true positives found among all actual positives and does not consider false positives or the overall ability to discriminate between classes. 2025-07-26 09:09:42,293 [INFO] Field changed at answer: '<p>When addressing overfitting in deep learning models, the goal is to help the model generalize better to new, unseen data. Increasing regularization or dropout rate are both established methods for reducing overfitting:</p><ul><li><b>Enhance the L1 and/or L2 regularization strength.</b> Regularization discourages the model from relying heavily on any one feature by penalizing overly complex weights, which promotes simpler models that generalize better.</li><li><b>Boost the dropout rate within your model.</b> Dropout randomly disables certain neurons during training, forcing the model to learn more robust features that do not depend on a few specific nodes, thereby lowering overfitting risk.</li></ul><p>The following options are not recommended in this scenario:</p><ul><li><i>Reduce the amount of L1 and/or L2 regularization.</i> Decreasing regularization makes the model more likely to memorize the training data, worsening overfitting.</li><li><i>Lower the dropout rate used in your neural network.</i> Lowering dropout increases the chance of neurons becoming too specialized, intensifying overfitting.</li><li><i>Expand the model's feature dimensionality.</i> Adding more features increases model complexity and the risk of overfitting, especially if your current problem is already one of overfitting.</li></ul><p><b>Tip:</b> In situations where your model excels on training data but suffers on validation or test data, always look for ways to regularize and add noise during training (like using higher dropout), rather than increasing complexity or removing regularization.</p>' \u2192 '<p>When addressing overfitting in deep learning models, the goal is to help the model generalize better to new, unseen data. 2025-07-26 09:09:43,377 [INFO] Field changed at answer: '<p>For categorical features with a large number of categories (often called 'high cardinality'), using <b>Target encoding using mean transformation along with smoothing</b> is the most effective approach.</p><p><i>One-hot encoding</i> can create a huge number of additional columns when there are many unique values, leading to a sparse dataset, potential overfitting, and computational inefficiency.</p><p><i>Label encoding</i> assigns arbitrary integer values to each category, which introduces spurious ordinal relationships between categories that don't actually have any order. This can negatively impact model performance, especially with tree-based and linear models.</p><p><i>Target encoding using only the category mean without smoothing</i> can cause overfitting, especially when there are categories with only a few samples, as their mean will be noisy and less reliable.</p><p>The correct technique, <b>Target encoding using mean transformation along with smoothing</b>, assigns each category a value based on the mean of the target variable for that category, but also incorporates smoothing to blend the category mean with the overall mean. This reduces overfitting, especially for rare categories, and creates a more robust and compact representation of the categorical features. This method is well-suited for regression problems and high-cardinality categorical variables.</p><ul><li><b>Tip:</b> For categorical features with a moderate or large number of categories, always consider advanced statistical or target encoding approaches with smoothing to prevent overfitting and retain model generalizability.</li></ul>' \u2192 '<p>For categorical features with a large number of categories (often called &apos;high cardinality&apos;), using <b>Target encoding using mean transformation along with smoothing</b> is the most effective approach.</p><p><i>One-hot encoding</i> can create a huge number of additional columns when there are many unique values, leading to a sparse dataset, potential overfitting, and computational inefficiency.</p><p><i>Label encoding</i> assigns arbitrary integer values to each category, which introduces spurious ordinal relationships between categories that don&apos;t actually have any order. This can negatively impact model performance, especially with tree-based and linear models.</p><p><i>Target encoding using only the category mean without smoothing</i> can cause overfitting, especially when there are categories with only a few samples, as their mean will be noisy and less reliable.</p><p>The correct technique, <b>Target encoding using mean transformation along with smoothing</b>, assigns each category a value based on the mean of the target variable for that category, but also incorporates smoothing to blend the category mean with the overall mean. Introducing or increasing regularization (such as L1/L2 penalties) helps control model complexity, further reducing overfitting.</p><p>Incorrect approaches include <i>Reduce the number of combined features</i>, which may unnecessarily discard useful information, making the model underfit. <i>Boost the number of feature combinations</i> can actually make overfitting worse by increasing complexity. <i>Lower dropout rates</i> or <i>Reduce the impact of regularization</i> will both further increase the risk of overfitting, which is the opposite of what you want. As a rule of thumb, when a model performs better on training than test data, <b>increase dropout</b> and <b>regularization</b> are excellent options to improve generalization.</p><p><b>Tip:</b> Always monitor the gap between train and test accuracy/loss. Regularization techniques, such as dropout and L2/L1 normalization, are standard tools for reducing generalization error in neural networks.</p>' \u2192 '<p>The correct strategies to mitigate your model&apos;s poor performance on test data are <b>Increase dropout in the network layers</b> and <b>Add more regularization to your model</b>. 2025-07-26 09:09:59,379 [INFO] Field changed at answer: '<p>Lambda@Edge functions can be triggered at four primary CloudFront lifecycle events: <b>Viewer request</b>, <b>Origin request</b>, <b>Origin response</b>, and <b>Viewer response</b>. These trigger points allow developers to execute code at the edge, enabling dynamic selection of A/B test content without changing the web application's core codebase.</p>
<p><b>Why the correct choices are right:</b></p>
<ul>
  <li><b>Viewer request</b>: Occurs when CloudFront receives a request from an end user—ideal for handling content selection before the cache or origin is consulted.</li>
  <li><b>Origin request</b>: Triggered when CloudFront forwards a request to your origin (web server, etc.), useful when modifying headers or selecting content after cache miss.</li>
  <li><b>Origin response</b>: Initiated when CloudFront receives a response from the origin, which enables content modification right before it's cached or sent back to the user.</li>
  <li><b>Viewer response</b>: Happens just as CloudFront sends a response to the user, allowing final alterations or header manipulations before content delivery.</li>
</ul>
<p><i>CloudFront cache</i> is <i>not</i> a supported Lambda@Edge event. It does not represent a trigger point for Lambda execution; it's a storage mechanism where files are cached, but no code execution occurs directly at this phase.</p>
<p><b>Tip:</b> To perform advanced content personalization or A/B testing at the edge, use Lambda@Edge at the appropriate event hook that matches the logic you wish to apply. After testing, traffic is switched to the new environment. The same approach is often called Red/Black deployment (the terms are interchangeable, though Blue/Green is more common in AWS).<br /><br />The answer is not <i>A/B testing</i> as that approach involves diverting traffic between multiple application versions simultaneously to gather data or run experiments, which is not the case here. <i>Rolling deployment</i> refers to gradually updating instances within the same environment without using separate groups—here, the deployment is performed completely on the secondary ASG. <i>Canary deployment</i> involves releasing a new version to a small subset of users before a complete cutover, rather than switching all traffic at once.<br /><br /><b>Tips:</b> In the AWS context, Blue/Green and Red/Black both describe swapping between entire environments with zero overlap in user traffic; it guarantees easy rollback and minimal risk.</p>' \u2192 '<p>This scenario illustrates both a <b>Blue/Green deployment</b> and a <b>Red/Black deployment</b>. 2025-07-26 09:10:02,619 [INFO] Field changed at answer: '<p><strong>The correct answers are:</strong></p><ul><li><strong>The post_build phase is the appropriate place to perform the Docker push to Amazon ECR.</strong> In CodeBuild, it's standard practice to structure your buildspec.yml to build and tag the Docker image during the <b>build</b> phase, and then push it to Amazon ECR during <b>post_build</b>. This ensures the image is only pushed if the build succeeds.</li><li><strong>The aws ecr get-login-password command simply gives a token, but you also need to use it to authenticate Docker to ECR.</strong> Running <b>aws ecr get-login-password</b> by itself will only retrieve the authentication token. To log Docker in to Amazon ECR, you must use that token in the Docker login command.</li><li><strong>In the post_build phase, before pushing the Docker image, you must execute aws ecr get-login-password to log in.</strong> Before issuing <b>docker push</b> in the post_build phase, you have to authenticate Docker against ECR by using the <b>aws ecr get-login-password</b> in a Docker login command. Failing to do so will result in authentication errors when pushing your image.</li></ul><p><em>‘No authentication is needed if the IAM role grants ECR read-only permissions; CodeBuild automatically handles ECR access’</em> is incorrect because while the IAM role needs the proper permissions, Docker still requires explicit login—CodeBuild does not log Docker in to ECR automatically for you. <em>‘You should place the docker push command in the build stage, since post_build is only for cleanup activities’</em> is also incorrect—the build stage is intended for compiling, testing, and building artifacts. 2025-07-26 09:10:02,830 [INFO] Field changed at answer: '<p>The <b>first option</b> is the best and most scalable approach for handling multiple on-call groups working on different schedules. By creating an SNS topic per on-call team, you gain flexibility to notify only the relevant group for each shift and can easily update subscribers when teams or schedules change. The application acts as a smart router, receiving alarm notifications (via HTTP POST from an SNS topic triggered by CloudWatch alarms) and determining which group is on shift, then using the AWS SDK to send notification emails via the correct SNS topic.</p>  <p>The <i>second option</i> would notify all on-call groups regardless of schedule, which is not ideal for teams with shift-based rotation; it fails to deliver alerts to only the intended on-duty group and may cause alert fatigue.</p>  <p>The <i>third option</i> is convoluted and ineffective. 2025-07-26 09:10:17,111 [INFO] Field changed at answer: '<p>The main challenge with weighted routing policies in Route53 is the impact of DNS <b>Time To Live (TTL)</b>. When you update the DNS records to shift traffic between blue and green environments, the TTL setting determines how long clients cache the DNS response. This means that, even after you direct all new traffic to the green environment, some users may continue to connect to the blue environment if their DNS cache hasn't expired. This could slow down both the rollout of new environments and any potential rollback since old DNS responses may still point to the previous environment. <br><br><b>The correct response is:</b> The effectiveness of the transition to a new environment may be hindered by DNS TTL since clients can cache DNS responses, potentially extending connectivity to the previous environment beyond the intended switch.<br><br><i>'Using a weighted routing policy in Route53 is inherently too complex to operate within a CICD deployment pipeline'</i>: This is inaccurate; weighted routing is straightforward to incorporate in automation and pipelines.<br><br><i>'A routing policy that is weighted within Route53 is never appropriate in situations where a rollback is needed.'</i>: This is not entirely correct; rollback is possible, though DNS caching can make the process slower.<br><br><i>'Only Classic Load Balancers are supported for this approach; Application and Network Load Balancers cannot be paired with weighted routing in Route53.'</i>: Both Application and Network Load Balancers are supported with Route53 weighted routing.<br><br><b>Tip:</b> To mitigate TTL issues, use shorter DNS TTL values when deploying blue/green strategies with DNS-based routing.</p>' \u2192 '<p>The main challenge with weighted routing policies in Route53 is the impact of DNS <b>Time To Live (TTL)</b>. 2025-07-26 09:10:21,662 [INFO] Field changed at answer: '<p><b>Send events to an SNS topic, then subscribe each SQS queue to the topic and configure a filter policy for each subscription</b> is the best approach.<br><br>AWS SNS supports native integration with SQS, meaning each queue can independently subscribe to the SNS topic and receive a copy of every event. What's more, SNS subscription filter policies allow you to specify which events each queue receives—solving the requirement to deliver only relevant subsets to each downstream pipeline, and doing so without custom code.<br><br><i>Write events to an SNS topic, subscribe each SQS queue, and use a Lambda function in each pipeline to poll and filter events from its queue</i> is less efficient. Each SQS queue would receive all events, even the irrelevant ones, leading to unnecessary message processing and potential cost/waste.<br><br><i>Deliver events directly to an SQS queue, have a Lambda function extract, filter, and forward events to multiple SQS queues as needed</i> introduces additional Lambda invocation and forwarding complexity, increasing latency, cost, and operational burden. It doesn't leverage AWS-native filtering available through SNS.<br><br><i>Use EventBridge as the event bus, have a Lambda pull, filter, and distribute messages to different SQS queues in parallel</i> is more complex and typically unnecessary for straightforward fan-out and filtering to SQS queues. EventBridge is great for complex routing patterns, but SNS with subscription filters is simpler and better suited to this scenario.<br><br><b>Tip:</b> Use SNS subscription filter policies to route messages efficiently to only those SQS queues that need them—no Lambda code required.</p>' \u2192 '<p><b>Send events to an SNS topic, then subscribe each SQS queue to the topic and configure a filter policy for each subscription</b> is the best approach.<br><br>AWS SNS supports native integration with SQS, meaning each queue can independently subscribe to the SNS topic and receive a copy of every event. While useful, an extended alarm period gives more direct control over how quickly the scaling policies trigger.</p><p><i>Change the group’s termination policy to always remove the latest launched instance first</i> has no effect on reducing scale activity frequency—it only affects which instance is chosen when terminating, not how often scaling happens.</p><p><b>Tip:</b> To avoid unnecessary scaling actions due to short-lived spikes, always consider tuning the monitoring period of your CloudWatch alarms and review your scaling thresholds to align with real-world application behavior.</p>'
